scenes.visual: Brief title card: 'What Pushes the Four Arrows?' Keep the carried Bay window faintly visible and the four factor icons moving behind it.

scenes.tts: Scientists ask two separate questions about a factor. First, which living and nonliving parts are involved? Biotic factors are living parts, such as grass and big crabs. Abiotic factors are nonliving parts, such as temperature and salt. Second, is the change natural, human-caused, or both? A cold winter is abiotic and natural. A stone wall is abiotic and human-made.
scenes.caption: Scientists ask two separate questions about a factor. First, which living and nonliving parts are involved? Biotic factors are living parts, such as grass and big crabs. Abiotic factors are nonliving parts, such as temperature and salt. Second, is the change natural, human-caused, or both? A cold winter is abiotic and natural. A stone wall is abiotic and human-made.
scenes.visual: Keep the window central. GREEN grass and a RED adult crab slide under 'biotic: living'. TEAL thermometer and salt gauge slide under 'abiotic: nonliving'. Then add a separate second question beneath them: 'cause: natural, human, or both?'. Show a cold winter tagged 'abiotic + natural' and a GREY wall tagged 'abiotic + human'. Do not draw exclusive bins.
scenes.narration: Scientists ask two separate questions about a factor. First, which living and nonliving parts are involved? Biotic factors are living parts, such as grass and big crabs. Abiotic factors are nonliving parts, such as temperature and salt. Second, is the change natural, human-caused, or both? A cold winter is abiotic and natural. A stone wall is abiotic and human-made.

scenes.tts: Watch a nonliving factor act. During a very cold winter, more buried crabs can die before spring. Lab tests also show especially low survival in cold, low-salt water. Both conditions can widen the death arrow. They may also act together.
scenes.caption: Watch a nonliving factor act. During a very cold winter, more buried crabs can die before spring. Lab tests also show especially low survival in cold, low-salt water. Both conditions can widen the death arrow. They may also act together.
scenes.visual: A TEAL cold front lowers over the carried Bay window. A TEAL salt gauge also drops. Some BLUE dots fade into the RED deaths arrow. Label the response 'schematic'; do not show a measured population size or claim one factor acted alone.
scenes.narration: Watch a nonliving factor act. During a very cold winter, more buried crabs can die before spring. Lab tests also show especially low survival in cold, low-salt water. Both conditions can widen the death arrow. They may also act together.

scenes.tts: Now watch living and nonliving parts work together. Young crabs use grass and shallow water as refuge from bigger crabs. With less refuge, more young crabs may stay exposed. That can increase deaths from predation. Refuge changes risk, not certainty.
scenes.caption: Now watch living and nonliving parts work together. Young crabs use grass and shallow water as refuge from bigger crabs. With less refuge, more young crabs may stay exposed. That can increase deaths from predation. Refuge changes risk, not certainty.
scenes.visual: Warm the same cove. GREEN grass sways in shallow GREY water while small BLUE crabs shelter. A large RED crab moves in deeper water. Shrink the grass patch; leave exposed young crabs visible. Mark the change 'schematic' and keep 'may increase deaths' on screen.
scenes.narration: Now watch living and nonliving parts work together. Young crabs use grass and shallow water as refuge from bigger crabs. With less refuge, more young crabs may stay exposed. That can increase deaths from predation. Refuge changes risk, not certainty.

scenes.tts: Suppose a stone wall replaces a gently sloping shore. The shallow refuge becomes smaller. Which population arrow could change first, and in which direction? Think in arrows, not labels.
scenes.caption: Suppose a stone wall replaces a gently sloping shore. The shallow refuge becomes smaller. Which population arrow could change first, and in which direction? Think in arrows, not labels.
scenes.visual: Transform the left shore into a GREY stone wall (YELLOW stays reserved for harvest). The shallow band and GREEN grass shrink. Hold all population arrows neutral. Show the question 'Which arrow could change first?' without revealing an answer.
scenes.narration: Suppose a stone wall replaces a gently sloping shore. The shallow refuge becomes smaller. Which population arrow could change first, and in which direction? Think in arrows, not labels.

scenes.visual: Hold the changed shoreline and question. Water ripples, grass sways, and young crab dots drift slightly. Keep all arrows neutral and reveal nothing.

scenes.tts: The death arrow could widen if more exposed young crabs are eaten. The wall is not the only possible cause of change. It alters habitat, while cold, harvest, and other factors may change other arrows. That wording keeps the claim honest.
scenes.caption: The death arrow could widen if more exposed young crabs are eaten. The wall is not the only possible cause of change. It alters habitat, while cold, harvest, and other factors may change other arrows. That wording keeps the claim honest.
scenes.visual: Widen the RED deaths arrow slightly and label it 'could increase'. Keep question marks beside TEAL cold and YELLOW harvest icons. Never label the wall 'the cause'. Reset the cove before the next scene.
scenes.narration: The death arrow could widen if more exposed young crabs are eaten. The wall is not the only possible cause of change. It alters habitat, while cold, harvest, and other factors may change other arrows. That wording keeps the claim honest.

scenes.tts: Harvest is a human-caused loss. Overharvesting means removing a species faster than it can replace itself. Female crabs carry eggs for the next generation. Leaving more adults can support later births, but the other arrows keep moving. More adults do not guarantee more survivors.
scenes.caption: Harvest is a human-caused loss. Overharvesting means removing a species faster than it can replace itself. Female crabs carry eggs for the next generation. Leaving more adults can support later births, but the other arrows keep moving. More adults do not guarantee more survivors.
scenes.visual: Return to the Bay window. A YELLOW crab pot pulls BLUE adult dots into the RED loss arrow. Narrow that arrow under 'harvest limit'. Leave several adult dots inside; later, small BLUE dots appear near a births arrow. Label the sequence 'schematic'.
scenes.narration: Harvest is a human-caused loss. Overharvesting means removing a species faster than it can replace itself. Female crabs carry eggs for the next generation. Leaving more adults can support later births, but the other arrows keep moving. More adults do not guarantee more survivors.

scenes.tts: Sustainable harvest means taking only as many as the population can replace over time. A harvest limit can reduce one loss and leave more adults to reproduce. A harsh winter, poor refuge, or few new young can still slow recovery. So recovery is not certain. Managers keep measuring every year.

scenes.visual: Show the YELLOW harvest arrow feeding into the RED losses side while the BLUE births-and-arrivals additions stay visible. Label the comparison 'harvest no greater than replacement over time: goal'. Do not draw a separate replacement arrow. Keep the RED death arrow and BLUE arrivals arrow moving. Replace any guarantee symbol with 'recovery not certain'.

scenes.tts: A population graph shows what changed, not which factor caused it. To test a cause, compare the graph with measurements of that factor. Survey estimates, experiments, and models each add evidence. None makes every arrow stand still. Together, they narrow possible explanations.
scenes.caption: A population graph shows what changed, not which factor caused it. To test a cause, compare the graph with measurements of that factor. Survey estimates, experiments, and models each add evidence. None makes every arrow stand still. Together, they narrow possible explanations.
scenes.visual: Transform the cove into a schematic population curve beside three panels: 'survey estimates', 'controlled test', and 'model'. Connect each panel to factor icons with moving lines. Keep a question mark between any single factor and the curve.
scenes.narration: A population graph shows what changed, not which factor caused it. To test a cause, compare the graph with measurements of that factor. Survey estimates, experiments, and models each add evidence. None makes every arrow stand still. Together, they narrow possible explanations.

scenes.tts: Return to the shared window. Natural events and human actions can change the same additions and losses. Management can change an arrow, but not command the whole population. The balance still decides the direction of change.
